t: More than 900 statues were carved, mostly from the tuff of Rano Raraku, where 394 in varying states of completion are still visible; hundreds were moved to ahu platforms around the island's edge.

The Rapa Nui regarded the moai chiefly as the living faces of deified ancestors, and archaeologists suggest they were also symbols of religious and political authority charged with sacred spirit, or mana.

Every erected statue had fallen by the late 19th century, and about 50 have since been re-erected; the island's population was devastated by slave raids in 1862, and the site was listed by UNESCO in 1995.
dyk: The statues had eyes: in 1979 Sergio Rapu Haoa and a team of archaeologists reassembled fragments of white coral and showed that the eye sockets held coral eyes with black obsidian or red scoria pupils.
ev: Carving of the moai began, a tradition that lasted mostly until about 1500
Jacob Roggeveen arrived, and the statues still gazed inland across their clan lands; all those erected on ahu were toppled in the years after
Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars reported some last standing statues
Slave traders raided the island, and within a year those who remained were sick or injured and lacking leadership
The moai Hoa Hakananai'a was removed from the island; it is now in the British Museum
The Routledge expedition linked the designs on the statues' backs to the island's traditional tattooing
Sergio Rapu Haoa and a team of archaeologists showed that the eye sockets had held coral eyes
The Rapa Nui National Park, with its moai, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

f.made: The Rapa Nui, the Polynesian inhabitants of the island, carving mostly between 1250 and 1500; oral tradition points either to a class of professional carvers or to members of each clan
f.form: Monolithic figures with oversized heads and no visible legs, mostly of volcanic tuff from Rano Raraku, averaging about 4 metres in height and about 12.5 tonnes; the tallest erected, Paro, was almost 10 metres and 82 tonnes
f.where: Rapa Nui, where nearly half remain at the Rano Raraku quarry and hundreds stand or lie on ahu platforms around the coast; ten or more were removed, including those now in the Louvre and the British Museum
f.known: enormous heads with elongated noses and ears; red scoria topknots (pukao); coral and obsidian eyes; the quarry at Rano Raraku; the debate over how the statues were moved; their toppling; Hoa Hakananai'a in the British Museum
